title: B-tree vs LSM-tree storage engines
scopeHtml: Scope: B-tree and LSM internals, write/read/space amplification, compaction strategies, read optimisations, choosing between them.

notes.title: What a storage engine does
notes.html:
A storage engine is the part of a database that decides how bytes are laid out on disk and how reads and writes find them. SQL parsing and the network are on top; the engine is underneath. Two families dominate: B-tree engines (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, SQLite, Oracle, SQL Server) update data in place, and LSM-tree engines (RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB, ClickHouse parts) never overwrite; they append and merge later.

The core fact that drives everything: disks (even SSDs) are fast at big sequential reads and writes and slow at many tiny random ones. A hard disk does roughly 100 random IOPS but 150 MB/s sequential; a good NVMe does around 500k random IOPS and several GB/s sequential, but random writes still wear flash and cost more than sequential ones.

Worked example. 100,000 small writes/s on a B-tree means up to 100,000 random page updates/s (each page 8 KB or 16 KB). The same writes on an LSM become one sequential log stream of, say, 100,000 x 200 B = 20 MB/s, far easier for the disk.

Industry examples. Postgres and MySQL (B-tree) run most transactional apps. Facebook built RocksDB (an LSM) for flash and uses it under MyRocks (MySQL), and many systems (CockroachDB, TiKV, Kafka Streams state) embed it. Cassandra and HBase are LSM from the Bigtable design.

Everyday analogy. B-tree is a neat paper address book: you find the page and erase and rewrite the entry. LSM is a diary: you always add at the end, and once a week you tidy it into a sorted index.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "LSM is just faster". It trades read cost and background work for write speed.
  • Forgetting that the storage engine, not the SQL layer, decides write behaviour.

notes.title: How a B-tree works
notes.html:
A B-tree is a shallow, wide, sorted tree of fixed-size pages (8 KB in Postgres, 16 KB in InnoDB). Each internal page holds many keys and pointers to children (fan-out in the hundreds). Leaves hold the data (or pointers to it). Lookup walks root to leaf, so cost is the tree height, usually 3 to 4 levels even for billions of rows.

Insert: find the leaf; if it has room, add the key. If full, split the page into two and push a key up to the parent (possibly splitting upward).

            [ 40 | 80 ]                   <- root page
           /     |     \
   [10|20|30]  [50|60|70]  [90|95|99]     <- leaf pages (sorted, linked)

Height math: fan-out 300, 16 KB pages. Level 1 = 300, level 2 = 90,000, level 3 = 27M, level 4 = 8.1B keys. Four page reads find one of 8 billion rows, and the top 2 levels are always cached in RAM, so it is often 1 to 2 real disk reads.

Safety: the write-ahead log (WAL). Updating a page in place is not atomic (a crash mid-write leaves a torn page). So the engine first appends the change to the WAL (sequential, fsync'd), then updates the page in memory (buffer pool) and flushes it later. After a crash it replays the WAL. Postgres also writes a full-page image after each checkpoint (full_page_writes) to protect against torn pages.

Industry examples. InnoDB clusters rows in the primary-key B-tree (the table IS the index); Postgres stores rows in a separate heap and indexes point at heap positions (ctid). SQLite and LMDB are also B-tree based.

Decision gravity. Choosing the engine is a deep one-way door: you cannot switch a Postgres to an LSM without migrating data. In MySQL, per-table engine choice (InnoDB vs MyRocks) is possible but a rebuild.

Everyday analogy. A library where books are sorted on shelves with a signpost tree at the door; adding a book to a full shelf means splitting it into two shelves.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the WAL; "in-place" does not mean "unsafe".
  • Random UUID keys cause random leaf inserts and splits; sequential keys append at the right edge.
  • Assuming leaves are always packed; page splits leave them about 50 to 70 percent full on average.

notes.title: How an LSM-tree works
notes.html:
An LSM-tree (log-structured merge tree) turns random writes into sequential ones by buffering in memory and writing sorted immutable files.

Write path:

  1. Append the record to the WAL (commit log) for durability.
  2. Insert it into the memtable, an in-memory sorted structure (skip list or red-black tree).
  3. When the memtable reaches a size (e.g. 64 MB), freeze it and flush it as an SSTable (sorted string table) on disk: sorted, immutable, with an index block and a Bloom filter.
  4. Background compaction merges SSTables, dropping overwritten and deleted entries.

Read path: check memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest until the key is found. Bloom filters (a compact probabilistic set, about 10 bits per key gives roughly 1 percent false positives) let the engine skip files that definitely do not contain the key.

Deletes write a tombstone marker; the data is physically removed only when compaction reaches it.

Worked example (RocksDB-like). Memtable 64 MB, key+value about 200 B: about 320,000 records per memtable. At 50,000 writes/s a memtable fills in about 6.4 s and flushes as one 64 MB sequential file. Level sizes grow by a factor of 10 (L1 = 256 MB, L2 = 2.5 GB, L3 = 25 GB, L4 = 250 GB).

Industry examples. Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, RocksDB, LevelDB, Bigtable, and the storage inside CockroachDB (Pebble), TiDB (TiKV with RocksDB) and Kafka Streams use LSMs. InfluxDB and many time-series databases use LSM-like designs.

Everyday analogy. A pile of sorted notebooks: new notes go on a scratch pad (memtable); when full, you copy it neatly into a new notebook (SSTable); occasionally you merge several notebooks into one sorted notebook (compaction).

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that reads must check multiple files.
  • Thinking SSTables are updated; they are immutable.
  • Ignoring that the WAL is still required (memtable lives in RAM).

notes.title: Write, read and space amplification
notes.html:
Amplification is how much more physical work the engine does than the logical work you asked for. There are three, and you can usually improve two at the expense of the third (the RUM conjecture: Read, Update, Memory overhead).

  • Write amplification (WA): bytes physically written to disk per byte the app wrote.
  • Read amplification (RA): disk reads needed per logical read.
  • Space amplification (SA): bytes stored on disk per byte of live data.
B-tree LSM leveled LSM size-tiered
Write amp Medium to high (rewrite a 8-16 KB page for a 100 B change, plus WAL, about 10-30x) High (about 10-30x from repeated merging) Low (about 2-5x)
Read amp Low (1 to 4 pages) Low-medium (about 1 file per level, with Bloom filters) High (many overlapping files)
Space amp Low-medium (page fill 50-90%, bloat) Low (about 1.1x) High (up to 2x or more during merges)

Worked example. Change a 100-byte row in an 8 KB Postgres page: the engine writes the WAL record (about 100-200 B) and eventually the 8 KB page = about 80x for that one write if nothing else shares the page; batching many updates per page lowers the average. A leveled LSM with 10x level fan-out and 5 levels: every byte may be rewritten about 10 times per level in the worst case, commonly cited as 10 to 30x overall.

Why write amp matters on SSD: flash wears out by program/erase cycles. A drive rated for 3 DWPD (drive writes per day) on 1 TB allows 3 TB/day; an app doing 1 TB/day of logical writes at 20x WA writes 20 TB/day to flash and kills the drive in months.

Industry examples. Facebook measured and tuned write amp when building MyRocks, reporting big space savings over InnoDB on flash (public papers; confirm exact figures). Uber's engineering moved from Postgres to MySQL citing Postgres's write amplification on index updates (their 2016 post; well discussed and debated).

Decision gravity. The compaction strategy per table is a medium door: changing it triggers heavy rewrite I/O but no application change.

Everyday analogy. Rewriting a whole page of your notebook to fix one word (write amp), versus flipping through 10 notebooks to find a fact (read amp), versus keeping old copies of notes around (space amp).

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting amplification numbers as exact; they depend on config and workload.
  • Not mentioning SSD wear when discussing write amp.
  • Treating the three as independent; they trade against each other.

notes.title: Compaction strategies
notes.html:
Compaction merges SSTables to keep reads fast and reclaim space; it is the main background cost of an LSM.

  1. Size-tiered (STCS): when you have N similar-sized files (say 4), merge them into one bigger file. Low write amp, but a key may live in many files (high read amp), and during a merge you temporarily need up to double the space. Good for write-heavy, rarely read data. Default in Cassandra.
  2. Leveled (LCS): files are organised in levels; each level has a size limit (10x the previous) and files within a level (L1 and below) do not overlap in key range. Reads touch at most one file per level; space amp about 1.1x; write amp high (about 10x per level). Default in RocksDB and LevelDB. Good for read-heavy or update-heavy data.
  3. Time-window (TWCS): group SSTables by time bucket (for example 1 day) and compact only within a window; drop whole expired windows with a TTL. Ideal for time-series and logs.
  4. FIFO: just delete oldest files (RocksDB). For caches and streams.
# Cassandra table compaction settings
compaction:
  class: TimeWindowCompactionStrategy
  compaction_window_unit: DAYS
  compaction_window_size: 1
default_time_to_live: 2592000   # 30 days
# RocksDB options (illustrative)
write_buffer_size = 67108864            # 64 MB memtable
max_write_buffer_number = 3
level0_file_num_compaction_trigger = 4
level0_slowdown_writes_trigger = 20
level0_stop_writes_trigger = 36
max_bytes_for_level_base = 268435456    # 256 MB
max_bytes_for_level_multiplier = 10

Incident pattern: compaction debt / write stall. Symptom: write latency suddenly spikes to seconds or writes are rejected. Metrics: pending compaction bytes rising, L0 file count above the slowdown trigger, disk at 100 percent utilisation. Cause: ingest outpaced compaction. Fixes: throttle ingest, add compaction threads, faster disks, bigger memtables, change strategy.

Industry examples. Cassandra clusters with TWCS for metrics and time-series; RocksDB-backed stores with rate-limited compaction to protect tail latency; ScyllaDB schedules compaction with a controller to keep latency steady.

Everyday analogy. Tidying a stack of notebooks: merge 4 small ones into one big one now and then (size-tiered), or keep a strict shelf system where each shelf has a size limit and overflow moves down (leveled).

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving size-tiered on a table with heavy updates; the same key lives in many files, reads slow down.
  • Forgetting that compaction needs free disk (keep 30 to 50 percent free with STCS).
  • Ignoring tombstone accumulation after mass deletes.

notes.title: Read optimisations in LSMs
notes.html:
Because a read may check many files, LSM engines add several tricks.

  • Bloom filters per SSTable: a "definitely not here" answer for about 10 bits per key; false positive about 1 percent. 1 billion keys x 10 bits = about 1.25 GB of filters; worth it.
  • Block cache and index blocks in memory so a lookup is one block read from the right file.
  • Sparse index: one index entry per data block (4 KB to 32 KB), not per key.
  • Prefix Bloom filters and range deletes for range scans.
  • Partitioned/two-level indexes when the index no longer fits in RAM.

Range scans are a weaker point for LSMs: the scan must merge-iterate across all levels. Point lookups of absent keys are cheap with Bloom filters; range scans are not helped by them.

Worked example. 5 levels, no Bloom filters: up to about 5 disk reads for a miss. With 1 percent false positive: expected extra reads about 0.05, so a missing-key lookup is near free.

Industry examples. Cassandra stores a per-SSTable Bloom filter and partition index summary in memory; RocksDB exposes bloom_filter and block cache settings; HBase uses Bloom filters per HFile.

Everyday analogy. Before searching 10 notebooks, you check a tiny sticky note on each cover saying "might contain Smith: yes/no".

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Bloom filters never give false negatives is right, but forgetting they do give false positives.
  • Expecting LSM range scans to be as cheap as B-tree leaf scans.

notes.title: B-tree vs LSM: choosing
notes.html:
B-tree: predictable low read latency, strong fit for transactions and read-heavy or mixed OLTP. LSM: very high sustained write throughput, better compression and space use, with background-work and tail-latency risks.

Aspect B-tree LSM-tree
Writes In-place, random I/O, WAL Sequential, buffered
Point reads Fast and predictable Fast with Bloom filters, more variance
Range scans Excellent (linked leaves) Good but merges levels
Space Page fragmentation, bloat; vacuum needed in Postgres Compact; compression works well on large sorted blocks
Tail latency Steady; checkpoint spikes Compaction/stall spikes
Locks/transactions Mature in-place MVCC, row locks Needs extra layers for transactions
SSD wear Medium-high write amp Depends on strategy

Worked example. A metrics system ingesting 1M points/s x 100 B = 100 MB/s. An LSM absorbs this on a few NVMe drives. A B-tree would need 1M random page updates/s; not sustainable without batching.

Decision gravity. One-way door at the platform level (Postgres vs Cassandra). Within an LSM, tuning compaction is a two-way door.

Industry examples. Facebook (MyRocks) cut storage roughly in half for some workloads vs InnoDB. Pinterest, Discord (ScyllaDB) and Netflix use LSM stores for write-heavy data. CockroachDB moved from RocksDB to its own LSM, Pebble, in Go to avoid CGo overhead and gain control.

Everyday analogy. A neat card catalogue (B-tree) versus a stack of daily logbooks you merge weekly (LSM). The catalogue is always ready to read; the logbooks accept new entries instantly.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking LSM for a read-heavy, latency-sensitive transactional workload.
  • Picking B-tree for a firehose of appends because "SQL is familiar".
  • Forgetting that tail latency (p99) is where LSMs hurt, not average.

notes.title: Variants and modern developments
notes.html:
Real engines blend ideas.

  • Postgres HOT updates and vacuum: an update writes a new row version in the heap; dead versions are cleaned by VACUUM. Without tuning you get table bloat.
  • InnoDB change buffer and doublewrite buffer: batches secondary-index changes and protects against torn pages.
  • Copy-on-write B-trees (LMDB, BoltDB): never overwrite; write new pages and flip a root pointer. Crash-safe without a WAL, single writer.
  • Fractal trees / B-epsilon trees (TokuDB): buffer writes in internal nodes.
  • WiscKey / BlobDB (key-value separation): keep keys in the LSM and large values in a separate log, reducing write amp for big values.
  • Columnar LSM (ClickHouse MergeTree): parts sorted by key, merged in background; used for analytics.
Write amplification relief, key-value separation:
  keys (small)   -> LSM tree (merged repeatedly)
  values (large) -> append-only value log (written once)

Worked example. 1 KB values with 16 B keys: separating values means compaction rewrites only 16 B keys plus a pointer, cutting write amp by large factors for big values, at the cost of extra read hop and value-log garbage collection.

Industry examples. ClickHouse MergeTree, TiKV's Titan, RocksDB BlobDB, Badger (Go) all implement variants of key-value separation or merge parts.

Everyday analogy. Keeping a small index card box and a separate archive room for the big documents.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing "B-tree vs LSM" as a pure either-or when real systems mix both.
  • Forgetting vacuum and bloat in Postgres when comparing space.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Storage engine = how bytes are laid out; B-tree updates pages in place with a WAL, LSM appends to WAL and memtable, flushes immutable SSTables and merges later.
  • B-tree height is 3 to 4 for billions of rows; page splits and random UUIDs cause fragmentation.
  • LSM read path: memtable, then SSTables newest first, with Bloom filters (about 10 bits per key, about 1 percent false positives) to skip files; deletes are tombstones.
  • Know the three amplifications: write, read, space; improving two costs the third (RUM).
  • Compaction choices: size-tiered (low write amp), leveled (low read and space amp), time-window (time-series, TTL), FIFO.
  • Write stalls and compaction debt are the classic LSM incident; watch pending compaction bytes and L0 file count.
  • Choose B-tree for mixed OLTP and predictable reads; LSM for write-heavy ingest; mind SSD wear and p99.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what happens when you write a key to an LSM-tree database like Cassandra or RocksDB, and then how a read finds it again.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know why LSMs are write-fast and where the read cost hides. Candidates who say "it just appends" usually cannot explain reads, deletes or the WAL.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I append the record to a write-ahead log for durability, then insert it into an in-memory sorted memtable and acknowledge. When the memtable hits a size like 64 MB it is frozen and flushed as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable. Reads check the memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest, using Bloom filters to skip files that cannot hold the key. Background compaction merges files and drops overwritten and deleted entries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Disks like sequential I/O, so an LSM turns every random write into a sequential one: one WAL append plus one memory insert. SSTables are never edited, which makes them easy to cache, compress and replicate. The price is that one key can exist in several places (an old value in an old file, a new one in the memtable), so reads must look in more than one place and the newest version wins.

Write: client -> WAL (fsync) -> memtable -> [full] -> flush -> SSTable (L0)
Read : memtable -> L0 files (newest first) -> L1 -> L2 ...
       each SSTable: Bloom filter -> sparse index -> one data block
Delete: write a tombstone; physically removed when compaction reaches it

The WAL is still needed because the memtable is RAM: after a crash the engine replays the WAL to rebuild it. Deletes and updates are just new records, so space is only reclaimed by compaction.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying SSTables get updated in place. They are immutable.
  • Forgetting the WAL and claiming the memtable alone is durable.
  • Forgetting tombstones, then being surprised that deleting data does not free disk.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens on a crash between flushes? -> Replay the WAL into a new memtable; WAL segments older than the last flush are discarded.
  2. Why is the memtable sorted? -> So the flush is a sequential write of an already sorted SSTable, and range scans can merge it with disk files.
  3. Why can a read of a missing key still be cheap? -> Bloom filters say "definitely not here" for each file at about 10 bits per key and roughly 1 percent false positives.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "writes are appended, so they are fast". The senior adds that the cost moved to reads and background compaction, names tombstones and Bloom filters, and says that p99 latency, not average, is where this design hurts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team deleted 80 percent of a Cassandra table and saw no disk relief for days because tombstones and data sat in files compaction had not yet merged.

questions.promptHtml: What are write, read and space amplification, and why can you not minimise all three at once?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the vocabulary used to compare storage engines. A senior should predict SSD wear and tuning direction from it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Write amplification is physical bytes written per logical byte the app wrote. Read amplification is disk reads per logical read, and space amplification is bytes on disk per byte of live data. They trade against each other (the RUM conjecture): leveled compaction gives low read and space amp but high write amp, size-tiered gives low write amp but high read and space amp.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each engine pays in a different place:

B-tree LSM leveled LSM size-tiered
Write amp medium to high (rewrite an 8-16 KB page for a 100 B change, plus WAL) high, about 10-30x low, about 2-5x
Read amp low, 1 to 4 pages low to medium high
Space amp page fill 50-90 percent, bloat about 1.1x up to 2x or more during merges

Worked example: a 100 B row change in an 8 KB Postgres page means roughly 100-200 B of WAL plus an 8 KB page flush, about 80x for that single write if nothing else shares the page. Many updates landing on the same page amortise this. Numbers are workload and config dependent; treat them as orders of magnitude.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting amplification as exact constants.
  • Ignoring SSD endurance, which is why write amp has a dollar cost.
  • Treating the three as independent knobs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does write amp hurt an SSD? -> Flash has limited program/erase cycles; a 3 DWPD 1 TB drive allows 3 TB/day, so 1 TB/day of logical writes at 20x amp wears it out in months.
  2. How would you lower LSM write amp for 1 KB values? -> Key-value separation (WiscKey, RocksDB BlobDB, TiKV Titan): compaction rewrites only keys and pointers.
  3. How do you measure it? -> Compare bytes written to the device (iostat, SMART) with bytes the app wrote; RocksDB reports compaction stats.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer defines the terms. The senior picks a strategy from the workload (write-heavy, rarely read means size-tiered; read or update heavy means leveled) and links write amp to drive lifetime and cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An ingest service sized by throughput alone burned through NVMe endurance far earlier than planned because nobody multiplied the logical write rate by the engine's write amp.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing storage for a metrics platform. 200,000 devices each send one 100-byte data point per second: 20 MB/s of ingest, about 1.7 TB/day. Queries are "last 24 hours for one device" (point-range) and a nightly rollup. Retention is 30 days. The team proposes Postgres because "everyone knows SQL". One engineer proposes Cassandra with TWCS. Budget: 6 NVMe nodes.
questions.promptHtml: Which engine family do you pick, with the numbers, and how reversible is the decision?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "LSM is faster for writes, so Cassandra." It gives no numbers, ignores the read pattern and does not mention operational cost or that the choice is a platform-level one-way door.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 200k points/s the peak or the average (burst factor sizes the cluster)? Do queries need joins or transactions (that pushes toward Postgres)? Is late or out-of-order data common (TWCS dislikes it)? What is the query latency SLO? Is the team able to operate Cassandra?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, so the equivalent is a risk-limited start: prototype both with a load test at 2x expected rate before committing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) LSM with time-window compaction fits an append-only, TTL-driven stream. (b) Postgres with partitioning by day plus batched COPY inserts might hold 200k rows/s per the math but needs bulk batching, and each index adds write cost. (c) A purpose-built TSDB may beat both.
  4. How I'd verify each: 200,000 points/s as single-row inserts in a B-tree is 200,000 random page updates/s plus WAL, too hot for a mid-size node without batching. Test with 10,000-row batches, measure WAL MB/s, checkpoint spikes, and p99 insert latency. For Cassandra measure pending compactions and p99 reads at the same rate.
  5. Root cause: The workload is write-dominant, append-only with expiry. LSM absorbs it as sequential I/O (20 MB/s raw, perhaps 60 to 200 MB/s after write amp), and TWCS lets whole 1-day windows drop on TTL without rewrite.
  6. Fix: Cassandra (or ScyllaDB) with TWCS, 1-day windows, 30-day TTL, partition key (device_id, day). Keep Postgres for device metadata and billing.
  7. Prevention: Alert on pending compaction bytes, p99 write latency and disk headroom (TWCS still needs free space for the active window).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not put raw points in Postgres only for SQL familiarity. This is a one-way door at the platform level, but I can reduce risk by keeping the ingest behind a queue so a second store can be dual-fed later. Within the LSM, compaction tuning is a two-way door.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Late data arrives up to 3 days old? -> It lands in old windows and forces re-compaction of closed windows; widen the window or write late data to a separate table.
  • Analysts want ad hoc joins? -> Ship rollups to a warehouse; do not bend the ingest store.
  • Reads dominate in 6 months? -> Then leveled compaction or a columnar store; re-test.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team picked a B-tree database for sensor ingest and hit 100 percent disk utilisation at a third of the target rate; the fix was batching plus moving the firehose to an LSM store while keeping the relational DB for metadata.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by familiarity or buzzword, no numbers.
  • Hire: derives ingest MB/s and explains random vs sequential I/O, picks LSM with TTL strategy.
  • Strong hire: also load tests, handles late data, states the reversibility and keeps SQL for the parts that need it.

questions.contextHtml: A RocksDB-backed service holds 2 billion keys over 5 levels. 60 percent of lookups are for keys that do not exist (a dedup check). Today bloom filters are disabled. p99 lookup is 18 ms, disk read IOPS are at 90 percent of the NVMe limit. The node has 64 GB RAM, 40 GB is used by the block cache. An engineer proposes buying more NVMe.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change, and how much memory does it cost?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more disks" or "increase the block cache". It does not see that each miss probes every level and that a tiny filter removes almost all of those reads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the keys point lookups only (filters do not help range scans)? What is the current block cache hit rate? Is there any slack RAM, and are index and filter blocks cached or competing with data blocks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If the node is at its IOPS limit, shed the dedup load or enable a short-lived in-memory cache for hot misses while the fix lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Misses touch up to 5 levels plus L0 files, each costing a read, so 60 percent of traffic is wasted I/O. (b) Block cache is thrashing because index blocks are evicted. (c) Compaction is competing for the same disk.
  4. How I'd verify each: RocksDB statistics for bloom.filter.useful and block.cache.miss, iostat -x for r/s and await, and per-level file counts. Run a read-miss benchmark with filters on.
  5. Root cause: No filters means roughly 5 or more disk reads for each absent key. With a filter of about 10 bits per key and about 1 percent false positives, the expected extra reads are about 0.05.
  6. Fix: Enable bloom filters, about 10 bits/key. Memory: 2 billion x 10 bits = 20 Gbit = 2.5 GB. Since the bottom level holds about 90 percent of keys, optionally skip filters on the last level (optimize-for-hits) only if most lookups are hits; here they are misses, so keep them everywhere. Keep index and filter blocks pinned in cache. 2.5 GB fits in the 24 GB of RAM not used by the cache.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard filter useful ratio, false-positive rate and p99 by hit vs miss.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not buy disks first. Filters only help point lookups, so range scans on this store need prefix filters. Do not go to 20 bits/key unless the false-positive rate still matters; returns diminish.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the keys are 20 bytes and values 50 bytes? -> The filter is still 10 bits per key, so ratio to data is small; the math is by key count.
  • What if filters do not fit in RAM? -> Partitioned filters and index blocks, loaded on demand and cached.
  • Does a filter help GET of an existing key? -> Slightly, it skips non-matching upper-level files.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dedup service sat at 90 percent disk IOPS for months; turning on 10-bit filters took it to 15 percent and removed a planned hardware purchase.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale hardware.
  • Hire: bloom filters with a correct memory estimate.
  • Strong hire: separates hit from miss, pins filter blocks, notes range-scan limits and verifies with statistics.

questions.contextHtml:
A Cassandra table stores user profile documents. Each user is updated about 20 times per day. 300 million users. The schema was copied from a logging table:

compaction:
  class: SizeTieredCompactionStrategy
  min_threshold: 4
  max_threshold: 32

Symptoms after three months:

nodetool tablehistograms users.profile
SSTables per read: p50=7  p99=19
Read latency p99: 85 ms (target 15 ms)
Disk used: 6.1 TB of 8 TB; compaction needs temp space

A teammate suggests adding more read replicas (reads are 70 percent of traffic).
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add replicas" or "increase the cache". It does not connect "SSTables per read: 19" to the strategy chosen for a heavily updated table.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the workload update-heavy on the same keys (yes, 20 per day)? How much free disk? Is the read rate consistent? Do we have a rolling-maintenance window?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Free disk headroom first (STCS needs up to double during big merges). Throttle or defer non-critical writes; do not trigger a major compaction at 76 percent full.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) STCS leaves overlapping files, so the same partition spans many SSTables. (b) Space amp is high because old versions of each profile linger. (c) Read repair or tombstones add cost.
  4. How I'd verify each: nodetool tablehistograms, nodetool tablestats (SSTable count, space used vs live), and sstablemetadata on a few files to see overlapping key ranges.
  5. Root cause: The same key is rewritten constantly, so its versions are spread over many similar-sized files that STCS only merges when 4 match in size. Read amp is the SSTables-per-read number.
  6. Fix: Short term: ensure free disk, then ALTER TABLE ... WITH compaction = {'class': 'LeveledCompactionStrategy'}. LCS keeps one non-overlapping file per level, so a read touches about one file per level and space amp falls near 1.1x. Long term: monitor SSTables per read and pending compactions.
  7. Prevention: Pick compaction by workload at schema review: STCS for write-heavy append, LCS for read-heavy or update-heavy, TWCS for TTL time-series.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: LCS raises write amp (about 10x per level), so check disk write throughput and CPU headroom. The migration rewrites data: stage it per node, never everywhere at once. I would not add replicas, which only multiplies the same slow reads.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Disk is 95 percent full? -> Compaction cannot run; add nodes or capacity before changing strategy.
  • Writes later spike 3x? -> Compaction can fall behind; watch pending compaction bytes and L0 count.
  • Why not TWCS? -> The data is updated, not time-ordered with TTL.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A profile table sat on STCS for a year; moving to LCS cut p99 reads from about 90 ms to under 15 ms and gave back about 30 percent of disk.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales replicas or cache.
  • Hire: recognises STCS vs LCS read amp for update-heavy data.
  • Strong hire: sequences the change around disk headroom, quantifies write amp cost and monitors it.

questions.contextHtml:
A RocksDB-based event store (leveled compaction) normally takes 40,000 writes/s at p99 5 ms. After a marketing event ingest rises to 90,000 writes/s. Within 20 minutes p99 write latency hits 4 seconds and some writes are rejected. Metrics:

rocksdb.num-files-at-level0        : 38   (slowdown=20, stop=36)
rocksdb.estimate-pending-compaction-bytes : 410 GB (rising)
rocksdb.is-write-stopped           : 1
disk util: 100%   cpu: 45%   mem: normal
rocksdb.actual-delayed-write-rate  : 16 MB/s

Reads are unaffected. A teammate wants to restart the process because "it looks hung".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart it" or "add CPU". Restarting does not reduce pending compaction and CPU is not the bottleneck; disk is.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 90k/s sustained or a burst? Is the write spike one producer we can throttle? Which disk type, and is another process sharing it? What are max_background_jobs and rate limiter settings?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Apply backpressure upstream: shed or queue ingest to bring writes below what compaction can drain (near 40,000/s). Do not restart; the stall is the engine protecting itself. If a rate limiter caps compaction I/O, raise it temporarily.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Ingest outran compaction: L0 file count crossed slowdown (20) and stop (36) triggers. (b) Compaction threads or I/O limited by config. (c) Disk saturated by something else. (d) A single huge L0-to-L1 compaction is serialised.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compaction stats (rocksdb.stats or LOG file), iostat -x (util 100 percent, write MB/s), per-level sizes, compaction thread count, and check whether L0 to L1 is the bottleneck.
  5. Root cause: Write rate exceeded sustainable compaction throughput. L0 files accumulated (each memtable flush adds one), reads got slower and the engine first slowed, then stopped writes to avoid unbounded debt. 410 GB of pending bytes means recovery takes time even after ingest drops.
  6. Fix: Short term: throttle producers, raise max_background_jobs/subcompactions if CPU and disk allow, enlarge memtables so each flush is bigger and L0 grows slower. Long term: faster or more disks, shard across more instances so each has less ingest, or consider a lower-write-amp strategy for this workload.
  7. Prevention: Alert on pending compaction bytes, L0 file count approaching the slowdown trigger and delayed-write-rate; load test at 2x peak; apply admission control at the API.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Raising the stop trigger only delays the cliff and hurts read latency. Disabling WAL or compaction rate limits risks data loss or tail latency for reads. Do not restart: recovery replays the WAL and starts with the same debt.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is CPU only 45 percent? -> Compaction is I/O bound; the disk is the limit.
  • Would more memtables help? -> They buy short bursts; sustained overload needs real throughput.
  • Could universal or FIFO compaction help? -> Universal lowers write amp at higher space and read cost; FIFO only if data is disposable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promotion doubled ingest on an LSM store; backpressure at the queue plus doubling compaction jobs recovered it in an hour, and the follow-up was a 2x load test in CI.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts or blames the network.
  • Hire: identifies L0/pending-compaction stall and applies backpressure.
  • Strong hire: sequences mitigation, explains why raising stop triggers is wrong, and sets alerts and capacity targets.

questions.promptHtml: How does a B-tree insert work, and why do random UUID primary keys hurt a B-tree table?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you connect the data structure to a real schema decision that teams get wrong.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A B-tree finds the leaf page for the key and inserts there; if the page is full it splits into two and pushes a separator key to the parent. With sequential keys inserts always hit the rightmost leaf, which stays hot in cache and fills pages. With random UUIDs inserts land on random leaves all over the tree, so the working set is the whole index, pages split everywhere and end about 50 to 70 percent full.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pages are 8 KB (Postgres) or 16 KB (InnoDB), fan-out is in the hundreds, so height is 3 to 4 even for billions of rows. In InnoDB the table is the primary-key B-tree, so a random PK scatters the rows themselves and every secondary index entry carries the PK. A page split writes two pages plus the parent and is logged to the WAL.

sequential key:  all inserts -> rightmost leaf (hot, cached, ~90% full)
random UUIDv4 :  inserts -> any leaf -> cache misses, splits, ~50-70% full

Fixes: time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, ULID, Snowflake), or a bigint surrogate key with the UUID as a secondary unique column. Postgres heap tables suffer less for the table but still for the PK index.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking splits are free; each is extra WAL and I/O.
  • Assuming UUIDv4 is fine on InnoDB because "the database handles it".
  • Forgetting that a larger PK widens every secondary index.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the WAL exist if pages are updated in place? -> A page write is not atomic; the WAL makes recovery possible and torn pages are handled by full-page images or a doublewrite buffer.
  2. Which two levels are effectively always in RAM? -> The root and the next level; so a lookup is often 1 to 2 real disk reads.
  3. How would you reduce splits during a bulk load? -> Load sorted, use a fill factor and build the index after loading.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "UUIDs are slower". The senior explains cache locality, fill factor, secondary index bloat on InnoDB and recommends a time-ordered ID, noting the privacy and ordering trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A table keyed by UUIDv4 doubled its insert latency once the index outgrew RAM, because each insert caused a random page read and a likely split.

questions.promptHtml: Compare size-tiered, leveled, time-window and FIFO compaction. When would you pick each, and what does each cost you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Compaction is the real tuning surface of an LSM. A senior chooses by workload and can predict the cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Size-tiered merges similar-sized files: lowest write amp, but high read amp and up to 2x space during merges, good for write-heavy data. Leveled keeps non-overlapping files per level with a 10x size ratio: low read and space amp, high write amp, good for read- or update-heavy. Time-window compacts only within a time bucket and drops whole expired windows, ideal for TTL time-series. FIFO just deletes the oldest files, for caches and disposable streams.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
STCS : [s][s][s][s] -> [M]  ... a key can live in many files
LCS  : L1 (256MB) -> L2 (2.5GB) -> L3 (25GB); one file per level per key
TWCS : [day1][day2][day3]  compact within a day; drop day1 when TTL ends
FIFO : drop the oldest file when size cap is hit

Selection rule: ask (1) are keys updated or only appended, (2) is there a TTL, (3) is the workload read-heavy. The operational costs: STCS needs 30 to 50 percent free disk; LCS drives sustained disk writes and can stall under ingest bursts; TWCS breaks down with out-of-order writes or TTL changes that mix windows; FIFO loses data by design.

compaction:
  class: TimeWindowCompactionStrategy
  compaction_window_unit: DAYS
  compaction_window_size: 1
default_time_to_live: 2592000

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• STCS on an update-heavy table (SSTables per read climbs).
  • TWCS with writes that carry old timestamps, defeating window isolation.
  • Not budgeting disk headroom for compaction.
  • Ignoring tombstones after mass deletes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does LCS have lower space amp? -> Within a level files do not overlap, so stale versions are removed as data moves down; about 1.1x.
  2. What is compaction debt? -> Pending bytes to merge; if it grows, reads slow and writes stall.
  3. Can you change strategy live? -> Yes, but it triggers heavy rewrite I/O; roll it node by node.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer names the strategies. The senior maps each to write, read and space amp, to disk headroom and to failure modes, and treats the switch as a medium-risk operational change.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A metrics cluster on TWCS dropped expired data with almost no I/O, while the same data on STCS needed days of compaction to reclaim space.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager says: "We are building chat history storage. It must scale to 50 million users and be fast." Nothing else is specified. The team is split: Postgres or Cassandra/ScyllaDB.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a database in the first sentence. Strong candidates ask what "fast" and "scale" mean in numbers before naming any engine.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: DAU and messages per user per day (writes)? Read pattern: open a conversation and read the latest 50 (a range scan on (conversation_id, time))? Retention and edit/delete behaviour? Multi-region? Do we need transactions across conversations? Latency SLO at p99?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; the equivalent is writing the assumptions down and getting sign-off.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Assume 50M users, 20 percent DAU = 10M, 40 messages/day each = 400M messages/day = about 4,600/s average, maybe 3x peak = 14,000/s. At 300 B each that is 120 GB/day, about 44 TB/year. (a) Single Postgres node handles 14,000 writes/s but 44 TB/year needs sharding. (b) An LSM store with partition key conversation_id and clustering by time fits both the volume and the access pattern. (c) Postgres with sharding (Citus or application-level) works if the team knows it well.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype the top 2 queries at 2x peak, measure p99 reads and writes, and cost out nodes.
  5. Root cause: The decision is driven by sustained write volume, a partition-local read pattern and data growth, not by "scale" in the abstract.
  6. Fix: Likely an LSM wide-column store for messages, relational DB for users and settings. If numbers were 10x smaller I would pick Postgres and avoid operating a second system.
  7. Prevention: Write an ADR with the numbers and the trigger that would make us revisit.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not pick the exotic store for 50 GB of data. Platform choice is a one-way door; keeping a message-store interface in the app limits blast radius.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Messages are edited often? -> Updates create multiple versions in an LSM; model edits as new rows with a version.
  • Strict ordering across devices? -> Needs a per-conversation sequence, independent of engine.
  • Full-text search? -> Add a derived search index, not the primary store.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team picked a distributed LSM store for 200 GB of data and spent a year on operations; a single well-indexed Postgres would have done the job.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: names a database first.
  • Hire: asks about workload, does volume math, ties access pattern to engine.
  • Strong hire: also states the break-even point, ADR and when to revisit.

questions.contextHtml: A RocksDB cluster stores 4 KB blobs (thumbnails with a 32 B key). The app writes 300 GB/day of logical data. The leveled LSM measures a write amplification of 18. Drives are 3.84 TB NVMe rated for 1 DWPD over 5 years, and the SMART data shows 40 percent of lifetime endurance used after 8 months. Finance asks why drives are being replaced so fast.
questions.promptHtml: Do the math and propose a fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy higher-endurance drives" without computing the cause or considering reducing amplification.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many drives share the 300 GB/day (per-node writes)? Are values updated or write-once? Is point read latency strict? Is the value-log GC cost acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Over-provision (leave 20 to 30 percent unused) and check that TRIM is enabled; that reduces flash write amp slightly. No data change needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Large values are rewritten at every level by compaction. (b) The WAL doubles writes. (c) Frequent small flushes or poor compression.
  4. How I'd verify each: Math: 300 GB/day x 18 = 5.4 TB/day to flash cluster-wide. Per drive depends on node count; with 6 drives that is 0.9 TB/day each, about 23 percent of a 1 DWPD rating (3.84 TB/day) before WAL, flash-internal write amp and replication multiply it. Check SMART "percentage used" and host writes vs NAND writes (verify the exact counters per vendor). Use RocksDB compaction stats to see bytes rewritten per level.
  5. Root cause: Compaction rewrites 4 KB values many times though only 32 B keys need sorting.
  6. Fix: Key-value separation (BlobDB or Titan): values go to blob files written once, compaction rewrites keys and small pointers. For 4 KB values and 32 B keys the LSM data shrinks by about 100x, so LSM write amp mostly disappears; the blob garbage collection adds its own writes (tunable). Cost: an extra read hop and GC work; range scans over values slow down.
  7. Prevention: Track WA and drive endurance in dashboards; capacity-plan on physical writes, not logical.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Switching to size-tiered cuts write amp but raises space amp; with big blobs the space cost is large. Do not just buy bigger drives: it treats the symptom. Test on a copy before moving production.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Values are updated often? -> Blob GC rewrites then increase; test the garbage ratio.
  • Values shrink to 200 B? -> Separation offers little; stay with plain leveled.
  • Why not a B-tree? -> It rewrites a 16 KB page per 4 KB change plus WAL; no clear win here.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A media metadata store lost half its drive life in a year; blob separation cut physical writes by about 4x and paid for itself within a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: replaces the hardware.
  • Hire: multiplies logical writes by write amp and compares to endurance.
  • Strong hire: proposes key-value separation with its read and GC costs and a test plan.

questions.contextHtml:
A Cassandra table inbox holds per-user notifications. A cleanup job deleted 70 percent of rows last night (about 4 billion rows). Today: disk usage did not fall, and a read path that normally takes 8 ms now times out for some users:

WARN  Read 1 live rows and 148320 tombstone cells for query SELECT ... WHERE user_id=? LIMIT 20
ERROR Scanned over 100001 tombstones; query aborted (tombstone_failure_threshold)
nodetool tablestats: SSTable count 412, pending compactions 9,800

A teammate says "the delete must not have worked, run it again".
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and how you fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Delete again" or "restart the nodes". It misses that deletes are writes and that tombstones live until compaction and gc_grace_seconds pass.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was it row deletes or TTL expiry? What is gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days; verify for the version)? How often is repair run? Which compaction strategy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop re-running deletes (each adds more tombstones). Tell the clients to page or bound queries by time so they skip dead ranges, and temporarily raise the tombstone threshold only as a last resort.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Tombstones are scanned on reads because compaction has not purged them. (b) Tombstones cannot be dropped yet because gc_grace_seconds has not elapsed or repair has not run. (c) Wide partitions concentrate dead cells.
  4. How I'd verify each: nodetool tablestats (tombstones per read), sstablemetadata for droppable tombstone ratio, nodetool compactionstats, and the table's gc_grace setting.
  5. Root cause: Deletes in an LSM are new records (tombstones). Data and tombstone only meet and vanish when compaction merges the files, and tombstones must be kept for gc_grace_seconds so replicas that missed the delete do not resurrect the data.
  6. Fix: Short term: let compaction progress (add compaction throughput), run a targeted compaction on the worst SSTables, and ensure repairs complete so tombstones can be purged. Long term: model expiry with TTL and time-window compaction so whole files drop, avoid mass deletes in a hot partition, and split big partitions.
  7. Prevention: Alert on tombstones scanned per read and pending compactions; run deletes in throttled batches.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lowering gc_grace_seconds to purge faster risks resurrecting deleted data if a replica was down longer. A forced major compaction on STCS can need huge temporary space.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just truncate? -> Fine for a whole table; not for per-user data.
  • Does a B-tree engine have this? -> No tombstone scans, but deletes leave dead tuples (vacuum) or empty space.
  • Would TWCS have avoided it? -> Yes if the cleanup was TTL by time window.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A purge of old notifications took a cluster to timeouts for a week; replacing it with TTL on time-window tables made the next purge free.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: re-run delete, restart.
  • Hire: tombstones and compaction explained, mitigates reads.
  • Strong hire: links gc_grace and repair, explains the resurrection risk and redesigns with TTL.

questions.contextHtml: A 24-node Cassandra cluster stores 90 days of click events on SizeTiered compaction, 65 percent disk full, 120,000 writes/s sustained, read SLO p99 20 ms. Retention is enforced by a nightly DELETE job. You want to move to TimeWindowCompactionStrategy with TTL. Business: no downtime, no latency regression beyond 10 percent, and the change must be rollback-able.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ALTER TABLE on all nodes." That triggers cluster-wide rewrite on a disk already 65 percent full and can cause an outage.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the table have mixed old and new timestamps (late events)? Can we create a new table and dual-write? Are TTLs needed on existing data? Is there spare disk or can we add nodes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Free space first (65 percent is too close with STCS temporary space): add nodes or clean up before touching the table.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: (a) ALTER causes a compaction storm and disk exhaustion. (b) Old data with no TTL stays forever in non-window files. (c) Existing data with mixed timestamps defeats the windowing for months. (d) Read latency regressions during compaction.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test on a staging cluster with a data sample, run compaction throughput throttling (nodetool setcompactionthroughput), and compare p99 before and after.
  5. Root cause: TWCS only helps when data is written into a window by time and expires by TTL; the old table's layout is not like that.
  6. Fix: Safest is a new table (events_v2) with TWCS (1-day window), default_time_to_live 90 days, dual-write from the app, backfill the last 90 days with throttled copy using the original write timestamps, flip reads, then retire the old table. Alternative in-place: alter one node at a time via a canary and watch metrics. Keep a rollback switch for reads.
  7. Prevention: Make compaction strategy part of schema review; alert on disk headroom, pending compactions and SSTables per read.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dual-write costs double write capacity temporarily; check headroom. I would not alter all nodes at once. Dropping the nightly DELETE only after TTL data is proven prevents tombstone floods.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Late events up to 5 days? -> Use a window that tolerates it or route late data to a side table.
  • Rollback after 2 days of dual-write? -> Reads still point to the old table; no data loss.
  • How do you prove parity? -> Sampled row counts and checksums per day.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team altered the strategy on a 70 percent full cluster and had to emergency-add nodes; the next time they used a new table with dual writes and nobody noticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: runs ALTER everywhere.
  • Hire: new table with dual write and backfill.
  • Strong hire: addresses disk headroom, timestamps, throttling, parity checks and rollback.
